state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Actually, alternate angles are only equal when the lines intersected by the transversal are parallel. In this case, since the lines are not parallel, angles \( p \) and \( q \) are not necessarily equal. Remember, alternate angles are equal only when the lines are parallel.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I see! So alternate angles are only equal if the lines are parallel. But how can I tell if the lines are parallel just by looking at them? Is there a way to figure it out?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: To determine if two lines are parallel, you can look for special angle relationships, such as corresponding angles being equal or interior angles on the same side of the transversal adding up to 180 degrees. Remember, parallel lines have specific properties that can help you identify them. Keep an eye out for these clues when analyzing geometric figures.

score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently states explicit rules (alternate angles equal only when lines are parallel, specific properties for identifying parallel lines), provides direct corrective feedback on the student's misconception, and clearly articulates procedural criteria for determining parallelism.
